name: THE I HATE TO SEE YOU BRIE-VE BUT I LOVE TO WATCH YOU GO BURGER

recipe.history:
Brie is France's most famous soft-ripened cheese, and its history stretches back to at least the eighth century when Charlemagne himself reportedly tasted it at a monastery near Meaux and declared it among the finest foods in his kingdom. Named for the Brie region east of Paris in the Seine-et-Marne department, the cheese is made from cow's milk and distinguished by its white, bloomy rind — a soft, edible coat of Penicillium camemberti mold that develops during the ripening process. Beneath that rind, the interior paste ranges from chalky and firm in young wheels to golden and almost liquid at peak ripeness, when a properly aged Brie will flow like warm butter when cut at room temperature. The flavor moves from mild and milky in youth to intensely earthy, mushroomy, and funky at full maturity — a complexity that has made it the standard-bearer of French fromage and a perpetual fixture on cheese boards from Paris to Los Angeles. True Brie de Meaux and Brie de Melun hold Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée status in France, meaning they can only be made in specific regions under specific conditions.

Brie's arrival in American cuisine accelerated dramatically in the 1980s, when the American palate began opening to imported European foods during a general food renaissance driven by travel, food media, and chefs returning from France with new ideas. It appeared first on restaurant cheese courses and then made its way into home kitchens, typically baked in puff pastry with jam as an appetizer. Its use in savory applications — on sandwiches, melted into eggs, draped over meat — came later and was largely driven by the artisan food movement of the 2000s. Brie on a burger is a revelation: when the wheel is sliced and laid over a hot patty, the rind softens and the interior melts into a warm, lush pool of creamy cheese that coats every bite. The earthiness of the rind, the rich fat content, and the subtle tanginess of well-aged Brie make it one of the finest cheeses a burger can wear. It pairs naturally with fig, apple, and caramelized onion — sweet, jammy elements that complement its depth the way the French have always known how to pair cheese with fruit.

I will never forget the first time someone served me a burger with Brie at a dinner party in a converted warehouse apartment in Brooklyn, around 2009, when everyone was cooking ambitious food at home because going out had become expensive and impractical. The host had sourced a wheel of real Brie de Meaux from a Murray's Cheese outpost and was slicing off thick wedges and laying them over the patties still on the grill so the cheese could melt with the lid down. When the plate landed in front of me, the Brie had oozed slightly over the edges of the patty, pooling against the bun in a way that looked almost painterly. I ate it and felt the particular emotion you feel when a casual meal turns out to be genuinely extraordinary — a kind of surprised gratitude that this combination of things exists and that someone thought to put them together. I have been chasing that burger ever since, and making my own version of it has gotten closer every year.

You will cook the patty to medium rare. This is not negotiable, and it is especially non-negotiable when Brie is involved. Brie at room temperature has an incomparable creaminess; Brie melted over a properly cooked 130-to-135-degree-Fahrenheit patty (54 to 57 degrees Celsius) takes on a liquid warmth that flows into the meat and mingles with the pink, iron-rich juices that only a medium-rare patty releases. An overcooked patty dries out, constricts, and stops releasing those juices — and when that happens, the Brie has nothing to work with, nothing to meld into. It just sits there, separated, like a sauce on a plate that has gone cold. Cook the patty right and the Brie becomes part of the burger. Cook it wrong and you have wasted some very good cheese.
ingredients: 3 large eggs (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
6 tbsp unsalted butter, softened and cut into pieces
8 oz ripe Brie, rind on, cut into 8 thick slices
1 cup dried figs, stems removed, roughly chopped
1 tbsp dry white wine or dry vermouth
instructions: 1. Make the fig-balsamic jam: Combine figs, balsamic vinegar, honey, water, thyme, and salt in a small saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring. Cook 15–20 minutes until figs are very soft and liquid is thick and syrupy. Remove thyme. Mash or blend to desired consistency. Cool and refrigerate until needed.

2. Make the caramelized onions: Heat butter and olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low heat. Add onions and a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring every 5–10 minutes, for 40–50 minutes until deeply golden and jammy. Add sugar and cook 5 more minutes. Deglaze with white wine, scraping up any browned bits. Season with pepper. Set aside.

3. Make the brioche bun dough: Combine yeast, sugar, and warm milk in a stand mixer bowl. Let bloom 5 minutes. Add 2 eggs and salt, then add flour. Mix with dough hook on medium 5 minutes. Add butter a few pieces at a time, waiting until each addition is incorporated before adding the next. Continue mixing 8–10 minutes until dough is smooth, shiny, and pulls away from the sides of the bowl.

4. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and refrigerate overnight or let rise at room temperature for 2 hours until doubled. Divide into 4 balls, flatten into bun rounds, place on a parchment-lined sheet, cover, and proof 1 hour.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush buns with beaten egg. Bake 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool completely.
6. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Form into patties 3/4 inch thick with a shallow thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt and pepper.

7. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Sear patties undisturbed 3 minutes. Flip and immediately lay 2 slices of Brie over each patty. Cook 2–3 more minutes. Check internal temperature — pull at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. The Brie should be melted and starting to ooze over the edges. Rest 3 minutes.
8. Split brioche buns and spread a thin layer of Dijon mustard on the bottom bun. Toast bun halves cut-side down in the skillet 60 seconds.

9. Assemble: Place a spoonful of fig-balsamic jam on the bottom bun over the mustard. Add a small mound of caramelized onions. Place the medium-rare, Brie-draped patty on top. Add frisée or arugula leaves. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt and the top bun. Serve immediately.
